brief: A tool caddy with a carry handle and divided bins for screws and bits.

requirements.evidence: Three cells in a row: the middle one is two storeys tall and has a bin on each side. Every open face is capped and the joints are bolted.
handle:0,0,1;top sits on cover:0,0,1;full;top at the top of the middle cell, so the caddy can be lifted from the middle. How much load it can carry is not verified: the configurator only checks fit.

requirements.requirement: Divided bins for screws and bits
requirements.evidence: bin:-1,0,0~hex-bin-full-div3 and bin:1,0,0~hex-bin-full-div3 give 6 compartments. Staging props (screws, nuts, standoffs and a hex driver) all show when viewed from above. The catalog has no bit prop, so no bits are shown.

finish.summary: I built a three-cell tool caddy in a row. The middle cell is two storeys tall, with a top cover and a carry handle on it. The cells on each side hold a full-depth bin split into 3 compartments, so there are 6 compartments in total for screws and bits. I capped every open face and bolted the joints. That brings it to 42 parts, a little over the usual limit of about 40. check_build found no rule issues and no mesh collisions. As staging I put screws, nuts and standoffs in the left bin and screws, nuts and a hex driver in the right bin. The catalog has no driver-bit prop. The configurator only checks fit, so how much weight the handle can carry is not verified.

lines.label: Edge cap · male, two stories tall
M6 x 25 socket head screw, ISO 4762

notes: Tighten every M6 to 2 N.m: HAND TOOLS ONLY, never a cordless driver. These bolts clamp printed PETG, not metal: at the bolt's own 10.4 N.m rating the head crushes the plastic under it and the joint fails silently, looking tight while holding nothing. Snug, then a nudge. Re-check the bolts after the first few weeks: PETG relaxes under load and the clamp will have eased.
